question: What constitutes the mining sector in Uganda and how are minerals classified under the Mining and Minerals Act?
answer: Mining is the process of extracting naturally occurring mineral substances from the earth or waters under geological processes (excluding petroleum). Under the Mining and Minerals Act, minerals in Uganda are classified into four main statutory categories: 1) Precious Metals: Gold, silver, platinum, palladium, iridium, osmium, rhodium, and rare earth elements; 2) Precious Stones: Diamond, emerald, ruby, sapphire, opal, amethyst, garnet, tourmaline; 3) Base Metals: Copper, cobalt, iron ore, tin, lead, zinc, and nickel; 4) Industrial Minerals: Sand, sandstone, granite, gravel, limestone, marble, clay, gypsum, phosphate rock, barite, dolomite, feldspar, and talc mined for domestic commercial use or industrial value addition.

question: Who are the key players in Uganda's mining sector and what licenses are required from government authorities?
answer: Key players comprise mineral extractors (large-scale commercial miners, medium-scale operators, artisanal/small-scale miners, commercial sand extractors, and rock quarry operators) and mineral traders/dealers. All operators must obtain statutory licenses from the Directorate of Geological Survey and Mines (DGSM) under the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development (MEMD), including Exploration Licenses, Mining Leases, Location Licenses, Artisanal Mining Licenses, Mineral Dealer's Licenses, and Sand/Quarry Extraction Permits. Operators must also secure NEMA environmental impact assessment approvals, local council permits, and a URA Tax Identification Number (TIN) before commencing operations.

question: What taxes, mineral royalties, and Withholding Tax rules apply to mineral extractors, sand quarries, and dealers in Uganda?
answer: 1) Mineral Royalties: Levied on the gross market value of extracted minerals under the Mining and Minerals Act and shared between Central Government, local district governments, sub-counties, and registered land owners; 2) Corporation Income Tax (CIT): 30% of chargeable income on net commercial profits; 3) Special Mining Deductions: 100% immediate capital deduction for depreciable assets acquired for mining exploration; deduction for contributions to an approved mine rehabilitation fund; recovery of costs for exploration work programs; and deductions for social infrastructure costs incurred in accordance with a mining lease; 4) Withholding Tax on Subcontractors: 10% WHT on service payments made to subcontractors in mining operations as a final tax (reduced from standard 15%); 5) Sand Extractors & Stone Quarries: Commercial sand pits and stone crushing operations must account for 30% CIT (or presumptive tax if turnover is UGX 10M–150M), PAYE on quarry workers, and 18% VAT if VAT-registered.

question: What customs duty and tax exemptions apply to imported mining equipment, exploratory machinery, and earthmoving gear?
answer: Under the Fifth Schedule of the East African Community Customs Management Act (EACCMA 2004) Part B Item 30 and EAC CET: 1) Exploratory & Geological Equipment: Specialized machinery, laboratory apparatus, deep core drills, and equipment for direct and exclusive use in mining exploration and geological development are exempt from customs import duty upon recommendation by the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development (MEMD); 2) Heavy Earthmoving Machinery: Excavators, bulldozers, wheel loaders, and stone crushing plants enjoy 0% import duty by tariff; 3) Heavy Tippers: Dump trucks exceeding 20 tonnes gross vehicle weight (GVW) enjoy 0% import duty for one year; 4) Temporary Imports: Heavy specialized mining rigs imported on a project basis enjoy customs duty suspension under security bond, discharged upon re-export.

question: What environmental and tax obligations apply specifically to sand extraction and rock quarrying businesses in Uganda?
answer: Under URA guidelines at https://ura.go.ug/en/category/tax-education/mining/sand-extractors-and-quarry-operations/: Commercial sand extractors (riverbed and wetland dredging) and stone quarry operators must: 1) Secure valid commercial extraction permits from the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development (DGSM) and local district authorities; 2) Obtain approved Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) clearance from NEMA to mitigate soil degradation and wetland loss; 3) Register for taxes with URA and obtain a 10-digit TIN; 4) Account for commercial sand/stone sales through EFRIS if VAT-registered, or pay annual presumptive tax based on gross sales; 5) Pay district local quarrying levies and statutory mineral royalties where gazetted.

question: Where can I find official URA tax guidance on the mining, mineral extraction, and quarry sector?
answer: Official publications are available under URA Tax Education > Mining at https://ura.go.ug/en/category/tax-education/mining/, including 'Overview of The Mining Sector' published on August 7, 2023 - 3:31 pm (https://ura.go.ug/en/overview-of-the-mining-sector/), 'Miners of Minerals' (https://ura.go.ug/en/category/tax-education/mining/miners-of-minerals/), 'Sand Extractors and Quarry Operations' (https://ura.go.ug/en/category/tax-education/mining/sand-extractors-and-quarry-operations/), and 'Petroleum Sector Q &A' (https://ura.go.ug/en/petroleum-sector-q-a/).
